lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 5 you set SMART goals. What does the M stand for? (Measurable.) Today: how to watch a performance, and help it improve.
Every skill has three phases. Preparation: getting ready (feet, eyes, arm back). Execution: doing it (the throw, the kick). Recovery: the follow-through, then getting ready again.
Watch with a checklist of teaching points. For an overarm throw: stand side on, arm back, step with the opposite foot, throw high, and follow through. Tick each point you see.
Use numbers too: count how many tries work. 6 successes out of 10 is 60%. A table shows which skill needs the most work: here, shooting.
Slow motion helps you see quick movements: film with a grown-up's permission, or watch a friend closely. Compare with a model: a good example of the skill.
Give feedback kindly and clearly: What went well (a strength to keep), and Even better if (one thing to improve). Be specific: not just 'good', but 'good: your arm followed through'.
Then improve: choose one point, practise it in a drill, and test again. Compare your results with your own last try, not with anyone else.
Try it in the world: watch a friend's jump in the game, and give one What went well and one Even better if. For real: record 10 tries at a skill, practise, and record 10 more. Next: food as fuel.

exercises.prompt: Put the phases of a skill in order.
exercises.hint: Get ready, do it, then finish.
It is the kind half of feedback.
exercises.explain: What went well: a strength the player should keep doing.

exercises.prompt: Feedback is most useful when it is specific.
exercises.explain: True: specific feedback tells the player exactly what to keep or change.

exercises.prompt: Bram's serve went in 7 times out of 10. What percentage is that?
exercises.hint: Per cent means out of 100: 10 goes into 100 ten times.

exercises.prompt: Match each phase to a moment of an overarm throw.
exercises.explain: Preparation: arm back, side on. Execution: step and throw. Recovery: follow through.

exercises.hint: Which one says exactly what to change?
choices: Even better if you step with your other foot.
exercises.explain: The specific one: step with the other foot.

exercises.prompt: Which skill should Zara practise most?
exercises.hint: Which has the lowest number of successes out of the same tries?
exercises.explain: Shooting: 4 out of 10 is 40%, lower than passing (70%) and dribbling (80%).

exercises.prompt: Slow motion can show quick movements you would miss.
exercises.hint: What is hard to see at full speed?
exercises.explain: True: slow motion shows each phase clearly.

exercises.prompt: Mimi made 12 of 20 catches. What percentage is that?

items: get ready for the next ball
exercises.hint: Before, during or after the main action?
exercises.explain: Preparation: eyes on the target, feet apart. Execution: swing, let go. Recovery: follow through, get ready again.

exercises.prompt: Tilly scored 5 of 10 shots before practice and 8 of 10 after. By how many percentage points did she improve?
exercises.hint: Turn each into a percentage first.

exercises.prompt: Put the improvement cycle in order.
exercises.hint: You need to know where you start before you improve.
exercises.explain: Watch and record, find one thing, practise it, then test again and compare.

exercises.prompt: A friend's standing jump lands short because the arms stay down. What is the best 'Even better if'?
exercises.hint: Which one names one clear change?
choices: Swing your arms forwards and up as you jump.
exercises.explain: Swinging the arms forwards and up adds power and distance.

exercises.prompt: Why compare a result with your own last try?
exercises.hint: Everyone starts in a different place.
choices: because other people do not matter
exercises.explain: It shows your own progress, which is what practice changes.

exercises.prompt: It is kind and helpful to give lots of things to improve at once.
exercises.hint: How many things can you practise at the same time?
exercises.explain: False: one or two clear points at a time are easier to practise.

exercises.prompt: In the table, what is Bram's success rate for serving, as a percentage?
exercises.hint: Turn successes out of tries into out of 100.
exercises.explain: 9 out of 20: 20 goes into 100 five times, 9 × 5 = 45%.
